title: Compact inference readings — running notes
content:
TL;DR: quick read notes & experiments to try for reducing tail latency and token cost on medium-length sessions (512–2048 tokens). Focus areas: smarter KV-cache eviction, prefix-aware batching, light quantization modes, and conditional routing for MoE-like shards. Goal is small, testable experiments to feed into Redwood Optimize suggestions and a short doc for the console team.

1) FlashAttention / kernel improvements
- Paper: FlashAttention (arXiv 2205.14135) — key idea: memory-efficient attention kernels reduce GPU memory and improve perf for long sequences.
- Takeaway: reducing attention workspace can enable larger per-GPU batch sizes without changing model weights.
- Where to try: dedicated/gpu pool with T4/RTX A5000 replicas for models we host (7B/13B).
- Quick test: compare throughput+latency for seq_len = 1024 with default kernel vs Flash-optimized kernel (same quant). Measure p99 and 95.
- Notes: watch for non-deterministic rounding and small accuracy delta on eval prompts (copy-sensitive).

2) KV-cache eviction heuristics (my main obsession)
- Short summary: naive LRU eviction is simple but may evict useful prefixes when many short sessions interleave with a few long sessions.
- Papers/blogs: several system posts, plus internal thread listing heuristics.
- Proposed heuristics to prototype:
  * Session-weighted TTL: give longer sessions longer TTL; weight TTL by recent token production.
  * Prefix-frequency caching: detect repeated prefixes across users and keep them sticky (cheap bloom filter to detect repeats).
  * Hot-path protect: keep KV for in-progress active sessions (last request < 5s).
- Metric to evaluate: per-token compute saved vs extra memory / hit rate broken down by session length. Track false-protect penalty (wasted memory).
- Experiment sketch: implement session TTL and prefix-frequency in the local dev KV cache (serving-runtime branch kv-tll-proto). Run 48h replay on trace subset (customer A) and compare token cost.

3) Quantization modes + perceptual quality checks
- Read: QLoRA / quant blogs. For 7B/13B/70B variants, 4-bit quant gives large cost win but may degrade name/entities.
- Practical plan: catalog 3 quant modes we can recommend in Redwood Optimize: "safe-4bit" (int4 symmetric w/ per-block bias preserve), "aggressive-quant" (int4 optimized), "mixed-8-4" (embs/kv in 8-bit, rest 4-bit).
- Quick checks: run the standard Redwood eval suite (50 prompts focused on factuality + code + math) and record BLEU-ish and failure modes.
- Note: add a simple quality gate in Optimize: if model sees >X factual failures on dev prompts, avoid aggressive quant for that route.

4) MoE and conditional routing trade-offs
- Reminder: Switch/SMoE papers show inference-time routing costs but can enable large capacity for particular tokens.
- Interesting thought: emulate conditional capacity by routing long-context/rare-token requests to a larger model variant instead of true MoE. Simpler operationally.
- Action: design a policy in the console: "route-if: session_length>1500 or token-entropy>Y". Test cost vs latency.

5) Retrieval latency vs freshness
- Notes from a few retrieval papers + our customer cases: RAG freshness matters more than perfect retrieval precision for chat-style UIs. That suggests caching retrieval results for short TTLs (30–120s) and using KV-cache to store retrieved docs per session.
- Experiment: small pilot with retrieval caching + cheap embed similarity threshold; measure helpfulness delta on prompts and end-to-end p95.

Open questions / TODOs (priority order)
- [ ] Implement session-weighted TTL in kv cache prototype + run 48h replay (owner: me).
- [ ] Add prefix-frequency bloom filter prototype (low RAM) and measure hit-rate lift (owner: Jordan).
- [ ] Define Evaluate set for quant-mode gating (owner: Mika) — 50 prompts per workload, label categories.
- [ ] Mock console policy for conditional routing (product sync in 2 weeks).
- [ ] Share early results in #inference-systems and add a short confluence doc with graphs.

Random notes / scratch fragments
- "sticky prefixes" could be keyed by hashing first N tokens of request; collision risk acceptable if bloom filter used.
- TTL formula idea: TTL = base + alpha * sqrt(session_tokens) — gives diminishing returns for very long sessions.
- Potential pitfall: prefix-frequency will favour boilerplate prompts ("You are a helpful assistant...") — need stoplist.
- In traces, ~12% of sessions account for 60% of tokens (confirm with sample) — heavy-tail impact on cache decisions.

Meeting bullets to share with console/product
- Objective: surface two new toggles in Console -> Model Routing: "Prefer larger-model for long sessions" and "KV-protect active sessions".
- Visuals: tiny chart of hit-rate vs memory cost, and schematic of prefix detection.

References & quick links
- FlashAttention paper & impl notes: https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.14135
- Switch Transformers overview: https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.03961
- Internal PR for kv-ttl prototype: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/472
- Slack thread (notes & data sample): https://redwood-internal.slack.com/archives/C01ABCDEF/thread/16423345
- Confluence draft for caching heuristics: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/INF/KV+Cache+Eviction+Notes

Final quick mental checklist before starting experiments
- pick representative traces (3 customers, small/med/large)
- ensure replay tool preserves timing and concurrency
- baseline metrics = current p50/p95/p99 latency, token cost, KV hit rate, memory usage
- record eval failure types for quant experiments (hallucination, entity-swaps, math errors)

Notes to self:
- Keep experiments small and repeatable (narrow surface), and prefer deterministic kernels first.
- Share early with Mika/Jordan to avoid duplicate work.

End notes: want to produce a 2-pager for product by end of next sprint summarizing 1) KV heuristics and 2) quant gating rules. This doc is my running scratchpad — expect typos and half-baked math.
